title: Can reachability diameter be approximated within a constant in near-linear time?
formal: For an unweighted directed graph $G=(V,E)$, define $D(G)=\max\{d_G(u,v):d_G(u,v)<\infty\}$. Is there an absolute constant $C\ge1$ and one randomized word-RAM algorithm that, on every input, returns an estimate $D(G)/C\le\widehat D\le D(G)$ with probability at least 2/3 in $\widetilde O(n+m)$ worst-case time? Here $n=|V|$, $m=|E|$, words have $\Theta(\log n)$ bits, and self-distances are included, giving D(G)=0 on an edgeless graph. The constant and the hidden logarithmic exponent are independent of G.
context:
A directed graph need not be strongly connected. Taking the maximum over all ordered pairs then produces infinity as soon as one pair is unreachable, concealing the lengths of the routes that do exist. Reachability diameter discards unreachable pairs. On a one-way path of five vertices it is four, even though most ordered pairs have no directed route.

A familiar undirected idea is to search from an arbitrary vertex and use a farthest vertex as a witness. Directionality breaks its guarantee. Consider a long one-way path and an extra sink reached by an edge from the first path vertex. Searching from that sink sees no other vertex; searching toward it sees only the first path vertex. Both searches reveal a distance of one while the reachability diameter can be arbitrarily large. This is an illustrative counterexample to that particular pivot choice, not a lower bound against every sampling algorithm.

There is also a distinction between additive and multiplicative error. An estimate within $k$ of the truth is useful when $D(G)$ is much larger than $k$, but gives little information when the diameter is small. The question requires a useful relative guarantee on every input, including graphs whose longest finite shortest path has only a few edges.

The 2026 paper makes this a fine-grained algorithmic question and leaves a substantial gap for unweighted graphs. Its strong hardness results for weighted graphs do not settle the unit-weight case.
why: This asks how quickly an algorithm can summarize the routes that actually exist in a directed network. I include it because it exposes a basic weakness of transferring undirected diameter intuition to directed graphs and provides a concrete benchmark for algorithms based on reachability, sampling, and shortcuts.
definitions: Distances count edges on a shortest directed path. The maximum concerns finite distances only; it is neither the longest simple path nor the maximum of the smaller of the two directional distances. $\widetilde O$ suppresses polylogarithmic factors. This card focuses the broader approximation–time tradeoff on near-linear running time.

progress.text: Theorem 9 gives an $n^{1/2+o(1)}$-approximation in near-linear time. Theorem 7 gives additive error $k$ in $O(nm/k)$ time; these guarantees leave the constant-factor near-linear target unresolved.

Corollary 5 conditionally excludes better-than-two approximation below the Boolean-matrix-multiplication exponent; its combinatorial version excludes truly subcubic combinatorial algorithms under combinatorial BMM. These results do not exclude every constant approximation.

answer_criterion: Give a randomized algorithm and one absolute constant C meeting the displayed guarantee in near-linear time on every directed graph, or prove that no constant approximation is possible with that time bound.

importance.reason: Relates directed reachability structure to near-linear algorithms and isolates a basic obstruction behind shortcutting and parallel graph computation.
